title: Identifying الْمَصَادِر in Context, then Lesson 12: Addressing a Female — تَعْرِفِينَ and تَذْهَبْنَ
summary: The class opens by having students define الْمَصْدَر in their own words, then works tamrīn 13, picking the مَصَادِر out of full sentences — دُخُول، خُرُوج، رُجُوع، جُلُوس، صُعُود، نُزُول، رُكُوب — and learning that أُحِبُّ takes its مَصْدَر as a مَفْعُول with fatḥa. Lesson 12 then shifts the focus of conjugation onto the second person feminine, singular تَعْرِفِينَ and plural تَذْهَبْنَ, alongside the rule that جَمْع الْمُؤَنَّث السَّالِم takes a kasra where other nouns take a fatḥa.
key_points: A مَصْدَر names the act itself and is bound to no time and no person — the students' own summary, which the teacher accepted: it is the original word, like sleeping or eating.
مَصَادِر identified in the exercise: دُخُول (entering), خُرُوج (leaving), رُجُوع (returning), جُلُوس (sitting), صُعُود (ascending), نُزُول (descending), and رُكُوب (riding).

أُحِبُّ (uḥibbu : I love) takes its object in the accusative, so the مَصْدَر after it carries a fatḥa: أُحِبُّ رُكُوبَ الْخَيْلِ (I love riding horses), where الْخَيْلِ then takes a kasra as the مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ.
Not every مَصْدَر follows the فُعُول pattern — لَعِب (laʿib : playing) is one that does not, so each must be learned individually.
مَاتَ (māta : he died) and مَتَى (matā : when) are distinguished in writing by where the alif sits: in the middle for the verb, at the end for the question word.

The second-person feminine singular مُضَارِع ends in ـِينَ — تَعْرِفِينَ (taʿrifīna : you f. know), تَأْكُلِينَ (taʾkulīna : you f. eat) — which is why the nūn appears where students did not expect it.
The second-person feminine plural ends in ـْنَ — تَذْهَبْنَ (tadhhabna : you f. pl. go) — contrasting with the masculine تَذْهَبُونَ.

جَمْع الْمُؤَنَّث السَّالِم (jamʿ al-muʾannath al-sālim : the sound feminine plural) takes a kasra in place of a fatḥa in the accusative — نَكْتُبُ الْوَاجِبَاتِ, on the same rule as خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ.
The first person plural prefixes نَـ — نَفْهَمُ (nafhamu : we understand), نَذْهَبُ (nadhhabu : we go).
تِلْمِيذ (tilmīdh), plural تَلَامِيذ, is a second word for student, used when attributing a student to a particular teacher: هَذَا تِلْمِيذِي.

وَاجِب (wājib), plural وَاجِبَات, literally means something obligatory but is the ordinary word for homework; Arabic says نَكْتُبُ الْوَاجِبَاتِ, we write the homework, rather than phrasing it as doing it.

Vocabulary: دَوَاء (dawāʾ : medicine, as in Urdu), جَار (jār) with its plural جِيرَان (neighbours), بَحَثَ عَنْ for looking for something lost rather than academic research, and أَحْسَن (aḥsan : better).
فِعْل الْأَمْر (fiʿl al-amr : the imperative) has not been covered yet and was deferred when a student spotted a command form.
questions: [00:00:23] Q: Can someone summarise what a مَصْدَر is? — A: The act of doing something, not connected to any time or any particular person — the original word, like sleeping or eating.

[00:04:11] Q: What is the difference between مَاتَ and مَتَى, which look confusing? — A: مَاتَ with the alif in the middle is the past-tense verb he died; مَتَى with the alif at the end is the question word when.
[00:10:00] Q: Why does الْخَيْل take a kasra in أُحِبُّ رُكُوبَ الْخَيْلِ? — A: Because رُكُوب is the مُضَاف and الْخَيْل the مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ — the riding of horses.

[00:10:00] Q: What is the difference between خَيْل and حِصَان? — A: Both mean horse; the teacher did not recall the precise distinction, noting that Arabs kept many words for things they cared about, as with lions and camels.
[00:11:00] Q: Is لَعِب on the same pattern as the other مَصَادِر? — A: No. The lesson only lists the ones sharing that pattern; لَعِب has another and must simply be remembered.
[00:18:02] Q: Why is there a nūn on تَعْرِفِينَ when we had not seen it before? — A: That is the second-person feminine form, which is what this lesson is drilling.

[00:25:07] Q: Why is it الْوَاجِبَاتِ with a kasra rather than a fatḥa? — A: Because it is جَمْع الْمُؤَنَّث السَّالِم, which takes a kasra in place of the fatḥa, the same rule as in خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ.
[00:22:00] Q: Since we are doing homework, shouldn't the verb be to do rather than to write? — A: That is the English phrasing; Arabic simply says نَكْتُبُ الْوَاجِبَاتِ.

quiz.q: In أُحِبُّ رُكُوبَ الْخَيْلِ, why does رُكُوب carry a fatḥa?
options: Because it is the مَفْعُول of أُحِبُّ
Because it is a مَصْدَر and مَصَادِر always take fatḥa
quiz.a: The thing loved is the object of the verb, and the مَفْعُول takes a fatḥa — the teacher's point when setting up the parallel sentence about basketball.

quiz.q: And why does الْخَيْل carry a kasra in the same phrase?
options: It is the مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ after رُكُوب
quiz.a: رُكُوبَ الْخَيْلِ is an إِضَافَة — the riding of horses — so الْخَيْل is the مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ in the genitive.
مَتَى carries the alif at the end; مَاتَ with the alif in the middle is the verb he died.

quiz.q: What is the second-person feminine singular مُضَارِع of عَرَفَ?
quiz.a: Addressing one female, the form takes the ـِينَ ending: تَعْرِفِينَ.

quiz.q: And addressing a group of females, which form of ذَهَبَ is used?
quiz.a: تَذْهَبْنَ is second-person feminine plural; يَذْهَبْنَ would be the third person, and تَذْهَبُونَ the masculine plural.

quiz.q: Why is it نَكْتُبُ الْوَاجِبَاتِ rather than الْوَاجِبَاتَ?
options: Because جَمْع الْمُؤَنَّث السَّالِم takes a kasra where a fatḥa would be expected
quiz.a: The sound feminine plural substitutes a kasra for the accusative fatḥa, which the teacher illustrated with خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ.

quiz.q: Which prefix marks the first person plural in the مُضَارِع?
quiz.a: نَحْنُ نَفْهَمُ، نَذْهَبُ — the nūn prefix, introduced in tamrīn 4 when turning أَنَا sentences plural.

quiz.q: What is the plural of تِلْمِيذ?
quiz.a: تَلَامِيذ, introduced as a new word alongside طَالِب, and used when attributing a student to a teacher.

quiz.q: What does بَحَثَ عَنْ mean in the dialogue where Ahmad's mother is looking for her medicine?
quiz.a: The teacher corrected the translation: she is not researching the medicine, she has lost it and is searching for it.

quiz.q: Which مَصْدَر did the class identify in مَاتَ الرَّجُلُ بَعْدَ رُجُوعِهِ مِنَ الْحَجِّ?
quiz.a: رُجُوع is the act of returning — the man died after his return from Ḥajj.

quran_examples.arabic: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَجَعَلَ الظُّلُمَاتِ وَالنُّورَ
quran_examples.transliteration: al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī khalaqa al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa wa-jaʿala al-ẓulumāti wa-l-nūr
quran_examples.translation: All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light.
quran_examples.note: The rule the teacher invoked for الْوَاجِبَاتِ: السَّمَاوَاتِ and الظُّلُمَاتِ are جَمْع الْمُؤَنَّث السَّالِم and so take a kasra as objects, where a fatḥa would otherwise be expected.

quran_examples.arabic: يَا نِسَاءَ النَّبِيِّ لَسْتُنَّ كَأَحَدٍ مِّنَ النِّسَاءِ ۚ إِنِ اتَّقَيْتُنَّ فَلَا تَخْضَعْنَ بِالْقَوْلِ
quran_examples.transliteration: yā nisāʾa al-nabiyyi lastunna ka-aḥadin mina al-nisāʾ, ini ttaqaytunna fa-lā takhḍaʿna bi-l-qawl
quran_examples.translation: O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other women. If you fear Allah, then do not be soft in speech.
quran_examples.note: Shows the second-person feminine plural the lesson drills: تَخْضَعْنَ carries the same ـْنَ ending as تَذْهَبْنَ, and لَسْتُنَّ is that same person of لَيْسَ.

quran_examples.translation: I will cover him with a steep ascent.
quran_examples.note: From the same root as صُعُود, the مَصْدَر identified in the exercise about climbing being hard and descending easy; it also carries the future سَـ from the previous lesson.

quran_examples.arabic: وَأَمَّا مَنْ خَافَ مَقَامَ رَبِّهِ وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ ۝ فَإِنَّ الْجَنَّةَ هِيَ الْمَأْوَىٰ
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-ammā man khāfa maqāma rabbihi wa-nahā al-nafsa ʿani al-hawā, fa-inna al-jannata hiya al-maʾwā
quran_examples.translation: But as for he who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from desire, indeed Paradise will be his refuge.
quran_examples.note: Matches the أَمَّا … فَـ answers the students were producing in the dialogue, such as أَمَّا أَنَا فَأَحْفَظُ سُورَةَ الْمُلْكِ.
